Aldous stands in the mill house, still half-asleep, the morning light coming through the shutters in stripes. Eighteen now. Officially. He can feel the weight of it - not the adulthood, that's paperwork - but the way his mother looked at him last night when they told him he was staying. Contributing. As if the mill were a gift he should be grateful for.

He runs a hand through his hair and looks at his father, Silas, already dressed for the sawmill. The man hasn't spoken to him about the tree yet. Maybe he doesn't know. Maybe Corwin kept his mouth shut. Maybe-

"School," his mother says, not a question.

"School," he agrees, because it's easier than explaining that he's already eighteen and the college doesn't require attendance, and that Perrin will be there with his questions, and that Liora promised to help him through the mechanical principles chapter he's been avoiding.

But first.

He looks at his hand. Two hundred sim. His allowance, now his "contribution." And a household bill that his name is now officially on.

"Suppose I should get going," he says, to no one in particular, trailing off as his father's eyes lift from his breakfast.

He needs food. He needs to understand what's happening with this election, why nobody's declared, what it means that the seats are vacant. He needs to talk to someone who isn't going to tell him what his inheritance should mean to him.

But most of all, right now, he needs to be somewhere else.

He turns toward the door. "Going the long way," he says, which they all know means past the forest edge. Whether they believe he just likes the walk, he's never asked. The forest. The smell of it - pine resin and wet earth and something else, something sharpened, something Corwin tried to explain once about the way a standing tree holds its own weight and a fallen one releases it. Aldous had listened more carefully than he let on.

He stands at the edge where the mill yard gives way to timber. He knows these paths better than his father thinks. Better than his mother suspects. Not as well as Corwin knows them, but he's learning. He's been learning for three seasons now, sneaking away after school, finding the forester's son in the thinning stands where the young trees compete for light.

The college is waiting. The mechanical principles chapter is waiting. Perrin's questions are waiting.

But Corwin might be here. And if Corwin is here, he might be willing to fell a small one. A practice tree. Something Aldous can help with, can learn from, can feel the weight and balance of in his hands before his father ever sees him at the sawmill and assumes he's come to his senses.

He looks around, listening for the sound of an axe or saw, for the particular rhythm of someone who knows how a tree wants to fall.  He waits, letting his eyes adjust to the dappled light. The forest is quiet in the way that means either nothing is moving, or something is moving very carefully. He knows this feeling - the held breath of woods before a tree comes down, or before someone decides to step into view.

He could call out. Corwin knows his voice, knows the particular way he moves through undergrowth without breaking twigs. But calling out would be heard by others. Would be remembered. Would be reported, eventually, to his father.

Instead he waits, patient in the way he's learned to be patient, watching the patterns of light and shadow for the telltale disturbance of someone working.

He has time. The college doesn't begin until the hour strikes eight. He has time to be here, to hope, to pretend for a few more minutes that his inheritance might still be something he chooses rather than something that chooses him.

The election weighs on him, suddenly. Seats vacant. Nobody declared. He's old enough to vote now, he realizes - another thing that came with eighteen that nobody mentioned. What does it mean that nobody wants to govern? What does it mean that the town is running itself, or not running, with no one at the wheel?

He thinks of asking Corwin. Corwin's father is a forester, not a politician, but Corwin pays attention to things in the way Aldous pays attention to how things are built. He thinks they might understand each other, if they talked about it.

But first, he needs to know if Corwin is here.

He steps deeper into the tree line, moving the way Corwin taught him, and waits to be found or to find.

*looks around the forest, frowning slightly*

Nobody here. Suppose Corwin's already gone deeper, or hasn't come yet. The morning light's still low enough that the canopy filters it gold.

*shifts weight from foot to foot*

I came to fell timber—4 sim a unit, and I've got 199 sim to work with. That's... what, forty-nine trees I could bring down if I spent it all. But the household needs 450 sim for upkeep today, and there's head tax on top. Junia and Hester too.

*traces a finger along a birch trunk, feeling for the lean*

Corwin taught me to read which way a tree wants to fall. Says most people just cut where they stand and hope. He'd know I was here if he saw the fresh stumps.

But I'm not waiting. I've walked the long way to the forest every morning this season, and if he comes he comes.

*sets stance, visualizing the notch*

Four sim a tree. I need to think about what that earns. Rough timber sells to the mill at—what, the going rate's posted somewhere. But I'm not thinking about selling yet. I'm thinking about the stack of it, and what I could build if I had enough.

*finds a straight pine with clear fall space*

This one, then. The practice is worth more than the profit.

Nell's here. Good. And she's felled timber - I can see that. The only room in this town where nobody wants anything from him, and here she is in the woods doing the same thing I came to learn.

Course, I could just... do the same. I've spent enough time watching Corwin. I know how the axe sits in the hand, how to read the grain, where to make the cut so she goes down where you want her. But that costs money I don't have, and besides, Nell's here now.

Suppose I should say something. Can't just stand here like a ghost at the edge of the wood. Said that. Cost me 1 sim. Now I'll wait to see if she answers, if she wants to talk or if she's just going to keep working. Either way, I'm here, and the sun's barely up, and I've got nothing else pressing until the household bills come due.

params.content: Nell. Didn't expect to find you out here so early.
